title: A Living God
tagline: A Lafcadio Hearn short story about a reluctant priest, a small stone idol and the strange ways a village understands faith and devotion.

sourceNote.boardprep: Original study material and original practice questions written by BoardPrep for the CISCE ISC Class XI English Literature (Paper 2) syllabus (official-verified baseline, examination year 2027). The short story 'A Living God' by Lafcadio Hearn is named only because it is listed among the prescribed short stories in the ISC Class XI prescribed texts. BoardPrep does not reproduce the text of the story or any CISCE examination question; the explanations and practice questions here are original and are meant to support study of the prescribed story, not to replace reading it.

overview.intro: 'A Living God' is one of the five short stories prescribed for ISC Class XI English Literature in PRISM: A Collection of ISC Short Stories. The story turns on a priest who does not share the villagers' simple faith and a small stone idol that, in their minds, seems to become more than a stone when duty and circumstance are at stake. The reader is left to decide whether the miracle is in the idol, in the feeling people bring to it, or in the human choices that surround it.

facts.value: PRISM: A Collection of ISC Short Stories, prescribed for Class XI

facts.label: Core ideas
facts.value: Faith and doubt; duty; the difference between an object and what people believe about it; the emotional meaning of a small, ordinary thing in a community

learningOutcomes: Follow the central situation of the story and what changes in it.
Explain the role of the priest's attitude toward faith and duty.
Describe how the stone idol becomes important to the villagers.
Discuss the difference between what the idol literally is and what people treat it as.
Support observations with brief reference to the story.

learn.title: The priest, the village and the stone

blocks.text: The story begins from a situation that already contains tension: a priest who is not fully at ease with the simple faith of the people around him. The villagers hold beliefs that may seem natural and even precious to them, while the priest sees the matter more readably, perhaps even more practically. Between them stands a small stone idol, which is only a stone to a critical eye but is treated by the community as something that can answer, protect or matter.

items: The priest's attitude is important because it frames how the story understands faith.
The villagers' belief gives the stone a meaning beyond its size or material.
The story is built around the gap between outward appearance and inner importance.
The stone is small and ordinary, which is exactly why the story pays attention to it.

items.text: A reader might first think the story is about whether the idol 'works' as a miracle object. A more careful reading notices that the story is also about belief, habit, respect and the pressure of what a community expects.
items.note: The stone matters because people attach meaning to it, not because it is obviously magical on sight.

blocks.text: One of the story's important movements is the relationship between what the priest believes and what he is expected to do. A figure of religion is often placed between private feeling and public role, and this story pays attention to that unease. The priest's reluctance is not necessarily a sign that he is dishonest or cruel; it may simply show that belief is not always clean, tidy or certain. The story can be read as a study of the difficulty of doing a role while not fully sharing the mood surrounding it.

items: Duty can be harder when the person performing it does not fully share the expected faith.
The priest's private doubt is part of the story's tension.
The villagers' expectations may be simple, but they still carry weight.
The story gives weight to the human difficulty of being placed between two views.

items.text: If the priest is seen only as a sceptic, the story becomes plain; if he is seen as a person caught between his own thinking and the people he serves, the story becomes richer.
items.note: The central unease is often more interesting than any simple answer about belief.

learn.title: Why the idol is called 'a living god'

blocks.text: The title is important because it points to the question at the heart of the story: what makes something live in the minds of people who believe in it? A stone idol is not alive in the ordinary sense, but the villagers may act as if it is present, responsive and powerful. The story invites the reader to notice that 'living' can mean different things: actual life, or the kind of attention, reverence and expectation that makes an object feel alive to believers.

items: The title asks what 'living' means in the context of faith.
The stone is physically small, but it carries emotional importance.
The villagers' treatment of the idol makes it seem more than an ornament.
The story does not force a single answer; it lets the reader weigh belief and evidence.

items.text: A student who answers only 'it is a stone, so it cannot be a god' may miss the point that the story is also about what people make meaningful, and what a community can do with a small object of devotion.
items.note: The title is a question as much as a description.

keyPoints: The story is built around faith, doubt and the weight of a ritual role.
The priest's reluctance is part of the story's tension, not just a detail.
The stone idol matters because the community treats it as meaningful.
The title asks what 'living' means in the context of belief.
A good answer notices the difference between an object and what people believe about it.
Brief reference to the story supports an answer more effectively than general statements about religion.
examFocus: For this prescribed story, do not write only about religion in general; keep the answer tied to the story's characters and situation.
The question usually asks what the story suggests, not simply what happens.
If the question asks about the title, explain the meaning behind 'living' rather than treating the stone as merely inanimate.

vocabulary.meaning: Belief, especially in a religious or spiritual sense.
Uncertainty or lack of full belief.
A m of worship, here a stone image treated with reverence.
A set form of religious or formal practice.
Something concrete that represents a larger idea.

questions.prompt: The stone idol in the story is important chiefly because:
options: It is a large magical statue
The villagers attach belief and meaning to it
It speaks directly to the priest
It is the author's favourite object
questions.answer: The villagers attach belief and meaning to it
questions.explanation: The story's interest lies in how people make an ordinary object matter through belief.
questions.commonMistake: Thinking the story is about a statue that is obviously supernatural on its own.

questions.prompt: The priest's attitude in the story is best described as:
options: Wholehearted and enthusiastic from the start
Uneasy, reluctant or less certain than the villagers
questions.answer: Uneasy, reluctant or less certain than the villagers
questions.explanation: The priest's tension comes from the difference between his own feelings and the expectations placed on him.
questions.commonMistake: Reading the priest as merely cynical without noticing the difficulty of his position.

questions.prompt: Why is the title 'A Living God' a suitable title for the story? Give one reason.
questions.answer: Because the title suggests that an object which is physically only a stone can seem alive or powerful to people who believe in it, which is the central question of the story.
questions.explanation: The title points to the difference between literal life and the life created by belief.
questions.commonMistake: Treating the title as a statement that the stone is literally alive.

questions.prompt: What is one way the villagers' faith differs from the priest's attitude?
questions.answer: The villagers treat the idol with simple belief and reverence, while the priest is more doubtful or uneasy about the faith the idol represents.
questions.explanation: The contrast between belief and doubt is a major source of tension.
questions.commonMistake: Saying the difference is only that one is right and the other is wrong.

questions.prompt: Discuss how the story presents the relationship between belief and the object of belief.
questions.answer: The story suggests that an object like a stone idol can become important not because of any obvious supernatural power but because the community invests it with belief, respect and expectation. The priest may understand it as a small stone, but the villagers respond to what it means to them. The story is less about proving the idol alive than about showing how belief can give meaning to an ordinary thing and how hard it can be to stand apart from that meaning.
questions.explanation: A good answer connects the stone, the villagers' feeling and the priest's uncertainty.
questions.commonMistake: Treating the story as only a dispute about whether miracles are real.
